title: WebAuthn / Passkey Authentication
subtitle: A server challenge, a signature made inside the authenticator, and a POST the server verifies against a stored public key. Step through it and see what the browser can — and cannot — show you.

steps.label: Click "Sign in with passkey"
steps.lede: The user starts the passkey ceremony. No password is involved; the proof will be a signature over a fresh server challenge scoped to this site.
steps.devtools: Open DevTools (F12) → Network, enable Preserve log, filter on Fetch/XHR. You will see two requests bracketing an invisible signing step.

steps.label: POST /assertion/options (fetch challenge)
steps.lede: The browser asks for authentication options. The server returns a random single-use challenge bound to a pending login, the RP ID the credential is scoped to, and which credentials it will accept.

jwt.title: PublicKeyCredentialRequestOptions
payload: Random, single-use (base64url); bound server-side to the pending webauthn_session cookie
Relying Party ID the credential is scoped to — the phishing boundary
Credential IDs the server accepts (username-first flow); empty for discoverable credentials
Authenticator must verify the user (biometric / PIN)

steps.devtools: Read the response under Preview: note challenge, rpId, and allowCredentials. A webauthn_session cookie ties the challenge to this attempt. Copy the challenge — you'll match it inside the assertion.

steps.label: Authenticator signs the challenge
steps.lede: navigator.credentials.get() hands off to the platform. The authenticator prompts for user verification, then signs authenticatorData plus a hash of clientDataJSON with the private key — all inside the device.
steps.codeTitle: In the page (not a network request)
steps.devtools: This is not a network request, which is why it has no Network row — you'll just see a pause. The browser scopes the credential lookup to rpId, so a phishing look-alike domain finds no passkey. The private key never leaves the authenticator.

steps.label: POST /assertion/verify (assertion)
steps.lede: The browser posts the assertion. The server looks up the public key by credentialId and verifies the signature, the echoed challenge, the origin, the rpIdHash, and the UP/UV flags and counter.

headers: sid=s%3AsynthSESSIONwebauthn0011; Path=/; Max-Age=1800; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax

jwt.title: What the server verifies in the assertion
payload: Must equal the issued single-use challenge
Must be an expected origin — this is the phishing check
rpIdHash must equal SHA-256(rpId); UP/UV flags set; counter checked
Verified over authenticatorData ‖ SHA-256(clientDataJSON) with the stored PUBLIC key
Maps to the account (discoverable-credential / usernameless flows)

steps.devtools: Open Payload and inspect the assertion fields. Decode clientDataJSON with the snippet and confirm type, challenge, and origin. You see the signature bytes but never the key that produced them. On success, Set-Cookie: sid=… begins an ordinary session.

steps.label: Signed in — nothing phishable
steps.lede: The server established a normal session cookie. No password crossed the wire and nothing reusable was exposed — a stolen assertion is bound to one challenge and origin.
steps.devtools: From here it is an ordinary session cookie: the browser replays Cookie: sid=…. Because the challenge is single-use and the origin is signed into clientDataJSON, a captured assertion cannot be replayed against another site or a later login.
